entries.name: ball lightning
entries.senseHere: A rare, unexplained glowing sphere seen during thunderstorms, lasting seconds and vanishing with or without a trace. It is distinct from ordinary lightning bolts and has no agreed scientific explanation despite thousands of reports.
entries.background: The term was coined by French scientist François Arago in 1837 and has since generated numerous competing theories and laboratory attempts at recreation, none fully accepted.

entries.name: François Arago
entries.background: 19th-century French astronomer and physicist who wrote an early scientific treatise on thunder and lightning, coining the term for this luminous phenomenon.

entries.name: COST Action P18
entries.background: A European-funded research collaboration proposal on the physics of lightning, involving around 30 researchers, whose consensus statement affirmed that ball lightning is a real phenomenon worth studying.

entries.name: Prairie Meteorite Network
entries.background: A US network of all-sky cameras that photographed the night sky continuously for over a decade to track meteors, incidentally capturing a vast archive later searched for ball lightning images.

entries.name: lightning location network
entries.senseHere: Systems of ground sensors that detect and pinpoint the time, location, and electrical strength of lightning strokes, used here to cross-check eyewitness ball lightning reports against real lightning data.
entries.background: BLIDS is Germany's lightning detection service and ALDIS is Austria's equivalent network; both arose from modern lightning-location technology developed in recent decades.

entries.name: cloud-to-ground stroke
entries.senseHere: A lightning discharge that travels between a cloud and the earth's surface, as opposed to one that stays entirely within or between clouds.
entries.background: This is standard atmospheric-electricity terminology distinguishing where a lightning channel terminates, used to classify the strokes correlated with ball lightning sightings.

entries.name: positive and negative lightning strokes
entries.senseHere: Lightning classified by the electrical charge it carries to the ground; positive strokes are rarer and typically far more powerful than the more common negative strokes.
entries.background: Most ordinary lightning is negative; positive strokes make up a small percentage of strikes but tend to carry much higher peak currents, which is notable in the ball lightning correlation data discussed.

entries.name: Wilhelm von Haidinger
entries.background: 19th-century Austrian geologist and mineralogist, a member of Vienna's Imperial Academy of Sciences, who personally witnessed and carefully documented a ball lightning sighting in 1868.

entries.name: Walther Gerlach
entries.background: German physics professor famous for the 1922 Stern-Gerlach experiment demonstrating quantum spin, who also witnessed and mathematically analyzed a ball lightning event in 1927.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
entries.background: 18th-century Baltic German physicist and member of the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences who died from a lightning strike while experimenting with atmospheric electricity, later mythologized as a ball lightning death.

entries.name: keraunoparalysis
entries.senseHere: A temporary paralysis or loss of sensation in a limb caused by a nearby lightning or ball lightning strike, distinct from lasting psychological trauma.
entries.background: The term describes short-term neurological effects of lightning exposure, a category of injury first carefully distinguished by neurologist Jean-Martin Charcot from long-term traumatic neurosis.

entries.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
entries.background: Pioneering French neurologist at the Salpêtrière Hospital in Paris and teacher of Sigmund Freud, known for studying nervous disorders including the aftereffects of lightning-related trauma.

entries.name: soil strike theory
aliases: Abrahamson and Dinniss soil strike theory
entries.senseHere: A proposed explanation that ball lightning forms when lightning vaporizes silicon-rich soil, creating a floating ball of burning silicon particles whose glow matches observed colors and elements.
entries.background: This theory, associated with researchers Abrahamson and Dinniss, is one of several competing physical explanations for ball lightning and was supported by spectral evidence in at least one recorded case.

entries.name: slitless spectroscopy
entries.senseHere: A photographic technique using a grating to spread captured light into its component colors without a narrow slit, allowing the chemical makeup of a glowing object to be identified from footage.
entries.background: This method let researchers analyze the light from a filmed ball lightning event to detect specific chemical elements, supporting the soil strike theory.
